name: Verteporfin (hair)
lead: Verteporfin (brand name Visudyne) is a light-activated drug approved for photodynamic therapy of abnormal blood vessels in the eye, for example in wet age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia and presumed ocular histoplasmosis.[1][2] Separately, laboratory research has examined it as an inhibitor of the YAP-TEAD interaction in the Hippo signalling pathway.[3]

In looksmaxxing communities, verteporfin is discussed as an experimental way to reduce scarring and to regenerate hair follicles in scarred or donor areas after hair transplant surgery, a use some posters describe as a route to repeated transplants.[4][5] This use is not an approved indication, and the human evidence for hair is limited to a few clinician-reported cases discussed online rather than controlled trials.

paras: Visudyne is indicated for predominantly classic subfoveal choroidal neovascularization due to age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia or presumed ocular histoplasmosis.[1] It is a two-stage treatment: the drug is infused and then activated by non-thermal red light, producing reactive oxygen species that damage the endothelium of abnormal vessels and occlude them.[1] Wikipedia also notes off-label use for central serous retinopathy.[2]
Grokipedia reports the original FDA approval date as April 12, 2000, with development by QLT Inc. and marketing by Novartis; that source is AI-generated.[6]

The label lists injection-site reactions and visual disturbances as the most common reactions (over 10 percent), and warns of extravasation, photosensitivity (patients are advised to avoid direct sunlight or bright indoor light for several days after infusion), decreased vision after treatment and anaphylactic reactions; porphyria is a contraindication.[1] In rats given roughly 40 times the human exposure, the label reports increased anophthalmia or microphthalmia.[1]
These data relate to the approved intravenous, light-activated eye treatment. No safety data from controlled studies of verteporfin injected into or applied to the scalp are available.

sections.h: Use in hair and scarring research
paras: Preclinical work has linked the YAP/TAZ and TEAD pathway to fibrosis and scar formation. A 2021 Science paper reported that preventing Engrailed-1 activation in fibroblasts, including by treating mouse wounds with verteporfin, allowed regenerative wound healing without a scar.[7] Studies in other tissues have implicated YAP/TAZ in kidney fibrosis and described YAP-TEAD disruption by verteporfin in cancer models.[3][8]
Wikipedia states that verteporfin is experimentally applied to reduce scarring in hair transplantation, citing the American Hair Loss Society, and gives no study details.[2]

No controlled clinical trial of verteporfin for hair growth or hair-transplant scarring was found. The human trials of verteporfin concern its approved ophthalmic use, including the TAP trials in macular degeneration and comparisons with ranibizumab.[9][10][11] Registered trials also exist in glioblastoma and breast cancer photodynamic therapy.[12][13]

Threads on looksmax.org present verteporfin as a possible route to "infinite" hair transplants and scarless surgery, citing a hair transplant surgeon's update on small case series, in which hair was reported to regrow in scarred transplant areas after nine months.[4] Another thread summarises laboratory findings on YAP/TAZ and argues the drug might reduce fibrosis in transplants, cosmetic surgery and acne scarring.[5] Other users in these threads raise cost concerns, with one reply stating a price of about 100 dollars per square centimetre.[4]
Community protocol posts also exist and describe self-experimentation with research-grade material; this wiki does not reproduce such instructions.

timeline.event: Visudyne approved by the FDA for choroidal neovascularization (per Grokipedia).[6]
Genes & Development paper reports verteporfin disrupting the TEAD-YAP complex in a cancer model.[3]
Science paper links Engrailed-1 inhibition, including verteporfin, to scarless wound regeneration in mice.[7]

lore.intro: Verteporfin is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a hair-transplant adjunct and scar-reduction compound, based on laboratory papers and a clinician's informal case reports.[4][5]

claims.claim: Verteporfin can regrow follicles in transplant scars and enable "infinite" hair transplants.
claims.believers: Posters point to a surgeon's report of regrowth after nine months in scarred FUT areas in a small number of patients and speculate that higher concentrations could do more.[4]
claims.experts: No controlled trial has tested this. Preclinical work shows verteporfin inhibits YAP-TEAD signalling and can reduce scarring in mouse wounds.[7][3]

claims.claim: Verteporfin enables scarless healing after cosmetic surgery and may remove acne scars.
claims.believers: A forum thread argues that inhibiting YAP/TAZ should reduce fibrosis and support regenerative repair, citing research papers.[5]
claims.experts: Evidence is limited to animal and cell studies on scarring and fibrosis; human data for cosmetic uses are absent.[7][8]

claims.claim: The compound is too expensive for most users.
claims.believers: One user states that it costs around 100 dollars per square centimetre treated.[4]
claims.experts: No published price analysis exists for hair uses; the approved product is a prescription ophthalmic drug supplied under regulatory controls.[1]

card.summary: Eye-disease photosensitizer that forums eye for scarless hair transplants; only lab and anecdotal data support that use.
card.note: Approved only as an intravenous light-activated eye therapy; hair use is experimental and unstudied in controlled trials.

quick.overview:
Verteporfin is a prescription drug used with a red laser to treat abnormal eye blood vessels. Online hair communities are interested because lab studies suggest it can block a signalling pathway tied to scarring.

Its use for hair transplant scars or follicle regrowth is experimental. Evidence is limited to mouse studies and a few surgeon-reported cases discussed on forums.
quick.mechanism: In its approved use it is activated by light to generate reactive oxygen species that close abnormal vessels. In the research relevant to scarring, it is thought to inhibit YAP/TEAD signalling, which affects how fibroblasts respond to injury.
quick.risks: The label warns of photosensitivity, extravasation, vision changes and anaphylaxis for the approved eye use. Safety for scalp use has not been studied in controlled trials.
